source: Moore & Healy (2008) The trouble with overconfidence
finding: Overconfidence is three different things: overestimation of own score, overplacement relative to others, and overprecision (too narrow certainty). They do not share one cause. Overprecision is the one that persists on all task difficulties.
numbers: PsycINFO search: 365 hits, 72% empirical. About 31% of empirical studies examined overprecision, about 5% overplacement.
limits: Review plus one new experiment; the three forms need separate measures.
agent_relevance: Our agent should not track one confidence-bias number. Track error in level (accuracy vs stated) and error in spread (too sure it is right) separately.

source: Moore & Healy (2008) Experiment: 82 students, 18 trivia quizzes
finding: Hard-easy effect reproduced inside one design: easy quizzes gave underestimation and overplacement; hard quizzes gave overestimation and underplacement. Difficulty flips the sign of error.
numbers: N=82 CMU students, 18 rounds of 10 items, three difficulty levels. Overestimation main effect of difficulty F(2,162)=42.53, p<.001, eta2=.34. Overplacement F(2,162)=24.88, eta2=.24. Mean overestimation 0.79 points on hard quizzes, underestimation 0.22 on easy (signs from text; PDF dropped minus signs).
quote: Participants overplaced their performances on easy quizzes
limits: Trivia quizzes with incentives (quadratic scoring, rank pay); lab students.
agent_relevance: A per-class pass rate from S0 is more informative than a global confidence offset: the right correction changes sign with difficulty.

source: Moore & Healy (2008) overprecision result in same experiment
finding: Even when level of estimates was accurate, people were overprecise: 90.5% nominal intervals contained the true score only 73.1% of the time. Hit rate was lowest (55.1%) when people knew little, higher (85.6%) once they had task feedback.
numbers: 73.1% hit rate vs 90.5% confidence; binomial p about 6 per million; prior phase 55.1%, interim 85.6%, posterior 84.4%. Earlier studies cited: 30% to 50% hit rate for 90% intervals (Teigen & Jorgensen 2005).
limits: Elicited full probability distribution over 11 scores, which is milder than interval tasks; different elicitation changes size, never produced underprecision.
agent_relevance: Overprecision shrinks with domain knowledge. Our agent's verbal certainty should be discounted most on out-of-domain items, least where it has a track record.

source: Moore & Healy (2008) review of elicitation effects
finding: Changing how the confidence question is asked changes the size of overprecision but never produces underprecision. Underplacement is common on hard tasks, shared burdens and rare events.
numbers: Example: average participant gave a 6% chance of beating another student on Amazon plant quiz (Windschitl, Kruger & Simms 2003).
limits: Secondhand summary of cited studies; I read the review text, not those papers.
agent_relevance: Format sensitivity means the elicitation prompt is a design variable to be tested, not a given.

source: Fischhoff, Slovic & Lichtenstein (1977) founding general-knowledge calibration (as cited in Moore & Healy 2008)
finding: Founding paradigm: people give the probability that an answer is right; confidence runs above accuracy. Cited by Moore & Healy as the typical hard-question overconfidence design.
numbers: No numbers read from the original in this session.
limits: Not opened; known only through the 2008 review text. Moore & Healy argue this paradigm confounds overestimation with overprecision.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on the classic effect size as a constant; it depends on item difficulty.

source: Merkle (2009) The disutility of the hard-easy effect in choice confidence
finding: Mathematical derivation: the hard-easy effect appears for almost any judge in realistic conditions (random error, regression), so seeing it does not show a particular cognitive mechanism.
numbers: Derives necessary and sufficient conditions; no sample. Conclusion: all types of judges show it in almost all realistic situations.
quote: all types of judges exhibit the hard-easy effect in almost all realistic situations
limits: Formal paper; says the effect cannot separate rival models of confidence.
agent_relevance: Rival theories (ecological, error models, bias) are not told apart by the hard-easy effect. Use other discriminating tests, e.g. random-sample versus selected items.

source: Prims & Moore (2017) Overconfidence over the lifespan
finding: Age is mostly unrelated to overestimation and overplacement. Overprecision (certainty that you are right) rises with age, strongest with probability elicitation, absent with confidence intervals and quantiles.
numbers: Study 1 age range 19 to 78, median 30 (mTurk). Replication N=200 Qualtrics panel, median age 50. Age with precision r(198)=0.137, p=.053 in replication; age with overprecision on shapes task r(198)=0.03.
quote: a lifetime of experience, rather than leading to better calibration, instead may increase our confidence
limits: Weak replication; effect depends on elicitation. Four direct replications plus extensions reported.
agent_relevance: Experience did not give better calibration, only more certainty. Longer exposure does not equal calibration; the agent needs feedback, not just more training text.

source: Li, Hale & Moore (2025) Is overconfidence an individual difference?
finding: Overestimation and overplacement are weak traits across tasks (average cross-task r about 0.1). Overprecision is more consistent across tasks within one measure but different measures of overprecision hardly correlate. Confidence is situational.
numbers: Study 1a N=379, 1b N=138 (10 months later). Average cross-domain r: overestimation 0.12, overplacement 0.10, overprecision 0.68. Test-retest: overestimation r=.29, overplacement r=.21, overprecision r=.49. Average correlation between different certainty measures r=.11.
limits: Online samples; measures differ across tasks. Authors contest claims of stable trait overconfidence (Lawson et al 2023; Binnendyk & Pennycook 2024).
agent_relevance: Confidence is context-bound, so a single global recalibration for the agent will not transfer; calibrate per task class.

source: Magnus & Peresetsky (2022) A statistical explanation of the Dunning-Kruger effect
finding: The Dunning-Kruger pattern (low scorers overestimate, high scorers underestimate) is fitted almost perfectly by a censored (tobit) model with boundary limits and regression to the mean, with no metacognitive deficit needed.
numbers: Fit to exam grade predictions of students in three exams; model fits the data almost perfectly. Cited: 42% of engineers rate themselves in top 5% (Zenger 1992); 94% of professors above average (Cross 1977).
limits: Rival to the metacognitive account (Kruger & Dunning 1999); a statistical account does not prove no metacognitive effect exists. Other replications (Gignac & Zajenkowski) were not opened.
agent_relevance: When checking whether the agent is worse at knowing when it is wrong on hard items, first control for regression and ceiling effects.

source: Sellier, Scopelliti & Morewedge (2019) Debiasing training transfers to the field
finding: A one-shot game-based debiasing training for confirmation bias transferred to an unannounced business case in graduate students.
numbers: N=290 graduate students in three programs; trained participants 29% less likely to choose the inferior hypothesis-confirming solution.
limits: Confirmation bias, not confidence calibration; training worked in people, not in a fixed model. Related to debiasing note 05.
agent_relevance: Shows human training can transfer; for an LLM the equivalent is a scaffold rule, not exposure.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large pretrained models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false items in the right format. Calibration improves with size and few-shot examples. Models can score their own sampled answers (P(True)), better when shown many of their own samples.
numbers: Models 800M, 3B, 12B, 52B. ECE with 10 equal-mass bins. RLHF policies look badly miscalibrated but T=2.5 largely fixes it on MMLU, MMLU True/False and TruthfulQA. P(IK) trained on TriviaQA generalizes partly across tasks but calibration out of distribution is poor.
quote: larger models are well-calibrated on diverse multiple choice and true/false questions when they are provided in the right format
limits: Pretrained models; format-dependent (adding none-of-the-above harms calibration). Accuracy and calibration not causally linked.
agent_relevance: Showing the model several of its own samples before it judges improves self-evaluation: supports using agreement across attempts (S3/S4) rather than one stated number.

source: Lin, Hilton & Evans (2022) Teaching models to express uncertainty in words
finding: A finetuned GPT-3 can output a verbal confidence that is calibrated and stays moderately calibrated under distribution shift, and tracks its own uncertainty rather than copying human examples.
numbers: CalibratedMath: 21 arithmetic tasks, trained on Add-subtract. Multiply-divide MSE for confidence: indirect logit 10.4 vs constant baseline 11.7. Multi-answer shift: indirect logit 22.0 vs baseline 37.4 MSE. (Verbalized finetune row not parsed from the layout text.)
limits: Needs finetuning; arithmetic only. Gain over constant baseline is small under one shift.
agent_relevance: A training-free scaffold cannot count on finetuning; use agreement measures instead.

source: Guo et al. (2017) On calibration of modern neural networks
finding: Modern deep nets are more overconfident than older ones; one-parameter temperature scaling fixes most of it.
numbers: CIFAR-100 ResNet-110: ECE 16.53% uncalibrated to 1.26% with temperature scaling. CIFAR-10 ResNet-110: 4.6% to 0.83%.
limits: Image classification, not language; needs held-out labelled data to fit T.
agent_relevance: Temperature fix lowers ECE without improving ranking of right versus wrong answers; do not read low ECE as good discrimination.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? (verbalized confidence, black box)
finding: Verbalized confidence from GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna, LLaMA-2 is overconfident and poor at telling right from wrong. Consistency across several sampled answers does better.
numbers: Five models, eight datasets. GPT-4 average AUROC for verbalized confidence 62.7% (chance is 50%). Average ECE of GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna above 0.377. GSM8K: AUROC 54.8% with one verbalized answer to 92.7% with 5 samples plus consistency. White-box vs black-box AUROC gap 0.522 to 0.605. Best methods cut ECE to 0.028.
quote: LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident, potentially imitating human patterns
limits: Gains from CoT largely come from shrinking the gap between accuracy and a constant 80 to 100% output, not from better discrimination (GPT-4 GSM8K, 93.6% accuracy, ECE 0.064 by saying 100% always).
agent_relevance: Direct support for consistency not stated certainty: measure agreement across independent attempts, log the stated number only as a weak signal. Few samples (about 5) already capture most of the gain.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration
finding: For RLHF models, verbalized confidence is better calibrated than the token probabilities; asking for several answer options before the confidence helps (a consider-the-opposite step from psychology).
numbers: ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 2 on TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA: ECE often reduced by a relative 50% or more versus token probabilities, with temperature scaling.
limits: ECE flaw: a guesser saying 50% every time on binary tasks has perfect ECE; accuracy-confidence match is not discrimination.
agent_relevance: Consider-the-opposite prompting is a human-derived intervention that carries over; but G1 says doubt only on signal. Use it at the elicitation step, not as a standing doubt loop.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) LLMs must be taught to know what they dont know
finding: Prompting alone gives poor calibration for open-weight models; fine-tuning on about 1000 graded examples with LoRA beats baselines and generalizes to new question types.
numbers: Training set about 20,000 examples from 16 datasets; effective with as few as 1000 graded examples. Open-ended MMLU: prompting ECE does not improve as base model improves; AUROC improves slightly, best prompting model still below the weakest fine-tuned one.
limits: Open models (LLaMA-2, Mistral, LLaMA-3); training required. Sampling methods give good calibration but weak discrimination.
agent_relevance: A scaffold-only agent will sit at the prompting end of this result; expect weak discrimination from stated confidence and rely on code-side checks (G3, G5).

source: Kuhn, Gal & Farquhar (2023) Semantic uncertainty / semantic entropy
finding: Counting meaning-distinct answers across samples (semantic entropy) predicts whether a free-text answer is right better than sequence likelihood, lexical similarity, or p(True). Wrong answers have more semantically different samples.
numbers: Metric is AUROC on QA; semantic entropy highest in the paper (values around 0.8; exact table numbers not recoverable from extraction). Authors argue Brier and ECE are unsuitable for free-form answers.
limits: Needs an equivalence step and several samples.
agent_relevance: Supports S4 harvest and grouping by behaviour: agreement measured in meaning space, done in code.

source: Steyvers et al. (2024/2025) What LLMs know and what people think they know
finding: Models are fairly calibrated internally, but default explanations make people far more confident in the answer than they should be. Matching the length and hedging of the explanation to the model's real confidence closes much of the gap. Longer explanations raise human confidence without adding information.
numbers: 301 Prolific participants, 40 questions each. Model AUC 0.751 (GPT-3.5), 0.746 (PaLM2) on MMLU choice; 0.781 (GPT-4o) short answer. People seeing default explanations: AUC 0.589, 0.602, 0.592. Model accuracy 55% GPT-3.5, 50% PaLM2 on the 350-question set; participants alone about 51%.
quote: relying on simple textual cues such as overall length
limits: Human trust study, not model calibration alone; length bias BF>25.
agent_relevance: The tone the agent uses carries confidence signals to readers even if inconsistent with real certainty. Output wording should be generated from the code-computed agreement score.

source: Zhou, Jurafsky & Hashimoto (2023) Navigating the grey area
finding: Putting confidence phrases in the prompt changes model accuracy: expressions of high certainty lower accuracy by 7% versus low-certainty phrases. Uncertainty markers are linked to answers on QA sites, certainty markers to questions.
numbers: 50 epistemic markers injected into QA prompts; accuracy varied by more than 80% across markers; high certainty cost 7% accuracy relative to hedged.
quote: highly sensitive to epistemic markers in prompts, with accuracies varying more than 80%
limits: Prompt-side, not output calibration; models mimic usage statistics rather than reflect epistemic state.
agent_relevance: Supports S1 input hygiene: a user's stated certainty or an I'm-sure hint is anchoring text to be moved out of the task block.

source: Yona, Aharoni & Geva (2024) Can LLMs faithfully express intrinsic uncertainty in words?
finding: Aligned LLMs answer with full decisiveness even when their own sample distribution is split. Prompting for hedges does not make state-of-the-art models faithful.
numbers: Faithfulness metric on [0,1]; vanilla baseline cMFG close to 0.5 for all models tested; no expressions of uncertainty generated without instruction. Confidence scoring prompt correlated 0.97 with author labels on 100 examples.
limits: Short factual QA; uses internal agreement as the confidence reference.
agent_relevance: Words cannot be trusted as a certainty channel; the agent's confidence should be derived from sample agreement, not from its own hedging.

source: Stengel-Eskin et al. (2025) DINCO: verbalized confidence with self-generated distractors
finding: Verbalized confidence is suggestible: the model gives high confidence to a claim and its contradiction. Normalizing confidence over self-generated alternatives plus consistency improves calibration.
numbers: Plain verbalized confidence ECE 0.240 vs 0.097 with DINCO in the intro example; beats best baseline (max sequence probability) by average ECE 0.077 on TriviaQA and 0.092 on SimpleQA; FactScore verbalized ECE 0.433 for Qwen3-8B. Cost 32% over self-consistency; scaling SC alone does not close the gap.
limits: Needs an NLI model; max-probability baseline has higher AUC on SimpleQA (0.800 vs 0.786).
agent_relevance: Matches G5: normalize probabilities over exclusive candidates in code. Coherence across rivals beats raw self-report.

source: Kale (2026) Future confidence distillation in LLMs (arXiv 2607.07626)
finding: Confidence after solving (judgement of learning) is better calibrated and more discriminative than confidence before solving (feeling of knowing). Linear probes on hidden states beat verbalized confidence.
numbers: Probes trained on 1800 samples per domain (60-40 split); on factual recall and logical reasoning calibration error nearly halved and AUROC up 0.09 to 0.15 over verbal confidence; math gains modest.
limits: Preprint, July 2026; needs hidden-state access.
agent_relevance: Ask for confidence after the attempt and its checks, not at the start (S0 gate should use class pass rates, not the model's pre-guess).

source: Cross-source check: calibration versus discrimination (Xiong 2023, Steyvers 2024, Kapoor 2024)
finding: Three independent studies agree: lowering average calibration error is easy (prompt tweaks, temperature), but separating right from wrong answers stays weak for verbalized confidence. Sample consistency and trained probes improve discrimination.
numbers: Xiong GPT-4 AUROC 62.7%; Steyvers human AUC 0.59 to 0.60 vs model 0.75 to 0.78; Kapoor: best prompting open model AUROC below weakest fine-tuned.
limits: Different metrics and tasks; synthesised by me from the three read papers.
agent_relevance: Report both ECE and AUROC in any agent test; ECE alone can be gamed by constant confidence.

source: Cross-source check: human-derived fixes on LLMs (Tian 2023, Zhou 2023, Xiong 2023)
finding: Human interventions partly transfer: consider-the-opposite and human-inspired prompts reduce overconfidence in LLMs, with diminishing returns for stronger models, and no single strategy wins everywhere. Hedging phrases also change accuracy.
numbers: Tian: relative ECE cut 50% or more; Xiong: no single prompt best across datasets and gains smaller for GPT-4; Zhou: 7% accuracy swing from certainty phrases.
limits: Synthesis across three read papers; none tests the same task.
agent_relevance: Keep elicitation prompts task-specific and benchmark-tested (G7).

source: Moore & Healy (2008) Bayesian overconfidence working paper (AoM version)
finding: Search snippet only: noisy estimates of self and other regress toward the mean; this predicts the hard-easy reversal. Not opened beyond the search excerpt.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat as the rival to bias accounts; prefer tests that vary noise and difficulty.

source: Krueger & Heck (2021) The end of overconfidence (review of Moore 2020 Perfectly Confident)
finding: Review of Moore's book: no single overconfidence, a family of effects; no single fix, a family of interventions. Simulations show overestimation and overplacement correlate because both depend on self-assessment.
numbers: Simulation of 5,000 cases with mean 50 and SD 15 for each variable (reported in review).
limits: Book review, not primary data.
agent_relevance: No universal debiasing step. Matches schema stance of per-class modes.
